list.listitem: Induction of labor is indicated when the health of the mother or fetus is at risk.A
The Bishop score is an effective cervical assessment tool to predict induction success.C
ACOG endorses either a ‘low-dose’ or ‘high-dose’ intravenous oxytocin regimen for women undergoing induction of labor.C
Prostaglandins (PGE2 or PGE1), both vaginal and oral, are effective for both cervical ripening and labor induction.B
Prostaglandins are contraindicated in patients with prior cesarean birth or prior uterine surgeries due to increased risk for uterine rupture.A

Induction of labor is defined as the use of medications or other methods to bring on (induce) labor. The goal of labor induction is to achieve vaginal delivery by stimulating uterine contractions before the spontaneous onset of labor.

The rate of induction of labor more than doubled from 1990 through 2010, from 9.6% to 23.8%, but declined slightly in 2011, and again in 2012 (to 23.3%). This slight decrease may be due to an increased recognition of neonatal morbidity and mortality associated with performing elective inductions at a gestational age <39 weeks.

There is controversy over whether induction at term is associated with improved neonatal outcomes or an increased rate of cesarean delivery, although the most recent evidence is supportive of induction over expectant management.

In a multicenter RCT of 619 women who were at least 35 years old at the time of expected delivery with a singleton live fetus in cephalic presentation, maternal and neonatal outcomes did not differ with induction of labor at 39 weeks of gestation compared with expectant management.

In a RCT of 162 women with a singleton gestation and a Bishop score of 5 or less, those randomized to induction of labor at 39 weeks gestation had higher cesarean delivery rates (30.5% vs. 17.7% for expectant management), although this did not reach statistical significance (RR 1.72; 95% CI 0.96-3.06).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 30 RCTs with 12,479 women concluded that labor induction at or beyond term compared with expectant management was associated with fewer all-cause perinatal deaths (RR 0.33; 95% CI 0.14-0.78) and fewer caesarean sections (RR 0.92; 95% CI 0.85-0.99) but possibly more operative vaginal births, based on moderate-quality evidence. The absolute benefit is small with a NNT to prevent one perinatal death of 426 (95% CI 338-1337). NICU admissions were lower, although the difference did not reach significance (RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.77-1.01), and fewer babies had low Apgar scores with induction. No important differences were seen for most of the other maternal and infant outcomes.

In the most recent RCT of labor induction at 39 weeks vs. expectant management until at least 40 weeks 5 days of gestation including 6108 low-risk nulliparous women, there was no difference in fetal morbidity between groups, but the induction group had a small decrease in cesarean delivery rate (18.6% vs. 22.2%; number needed to treat [NNT] = 28). However, only 27% of eligible women were enrolled and there was no specific induction protocol.

In a meta-analysis of 6 U.S. cohort studies in which elective induction at 39 weeks' gestation was compared with expectant management for nulliparous women without medical indications, authors found a lower rate of cesarean section delivery among the 66,019 women in the induction group vs. the 584,390 women in the control group (26.4% vs. 29.1%; relative risk [RR] 0.83; 95% CI 0.74-0.93). Induction was also superior to expectant management with respect to maternal peripartum infection (2.8% vs. 5.2%; RR 0.53, 0.39 - 0.82), neonatal intensive care admission (3.5% vs. 5.5%; RR 0.80; 0.72-0.88), and perinatal mortality (0.04% vs. 0.20%; RR 0.27; 0.09-0.76).

In a European RCT of 818 women with singleton fetuses whose estimated weight exceeded the 95th percentile, induction at 37 weeks to 38(+6) weeks gestation vs. expectant management resulted in lower mean birth weights (3831 g (SD 324) vs. 4118 g (392), respectively) and lower rates of shoulder dystocia but no differences in cesarean delivery or neonatal morbidity; no cases of brachial plexus injuries, intracranial hemorrhages, or perinatal deaths were recorded.

Induction is indicated when the health of the mother or fetus is at risk. When labor is induced for nonmedical reasons (i.e., living far away from the hospital or convenience of the parent or delivering physician), it is termed an elective induction. Elective induction should not occur at a gestational age <39 weeks.
Placental abruption.
Preeclampsia.

Premature rupture of membranes: In a RCT of 1838 women with preterm premature rupture of membranes at 34 to 36 6/7 weeks' gestation who were randomized to expectant management or immediate delivery, there was no statistically significant difference in the incidence of neonatal sepsis. Newborns from the immediate delivery group had increased incidence of respiratory distress and mechanical ventilation, and spent more time in the neonatal intensive care unit.
Postterm pregnancy.

Gestational hypertension: In a randomized trial of 403 pregnant patients with chronic hypertension or gestational hypertension, planned delivery at 38 0/7 weeks’ gestation had similar outcomes for mothers and babies as routine care at term, which could include planned birth at 39 weeks of gestation. A cohort study nested in a RCT concluded based on weak evidence that 39 weeks is the best time for delivery in patients with mild chronic hypertension.

Induction is more successful if the cervix is soft, effaced, dilated, and/or anterior in the vagina, and if the fetal head has descended.
The “Bishop score” is the cervical assessment tool most often used to predict induction success (see ).
A Bishop score of greater than 5 is considered to indicate a favorable prognosis for induction with pitocin alone, also known as a "ripe" cervix.

For patients with a Bishop score of ≤ 5, ripening can be accomplished by mechanical means (catheters/cervical dilators) or ripening agents (prostaglandin preparations). Note that prostaglandins are contraindicated in patients with prior cesarean birth, or prior uterine surgeries, due to increased risk for uterine rupture.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 96 RCTs investigating methods for cervical ripening during labor induction concluded that vaginal misoprostol was the more effective than oral misoprostol, Foley catheters or dinoprostone for achieving vaginal delivery within 24 hours, but had the highest incidence of uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes. Oral misoprostol was safer than vaginal misoprostol and had a lowest rate of cesarean deliveries.

Among women with a Bishop score <6 who were undergoing induction, concurrent use of oxytocin and Foley catheter vs. Foley catheter placement for at least 12 hours followed by oxytocin increased the rate of delivery within 24 hours for both nulliparous and multiparous women.

In one study of 180 multiparous women with intact membranes and cervical dilation of 2 cm or less who required labor induction, concurrent use of a Foley catheter balloon and oxytocin resulted in reduced time to delivery (mean 3.8 hours) and improved the rate of delivery within 24 hours (88% vs. 73%; NNT = 7) compared to sequential use. There were no significant differences in maternal or neonatal morbidities reported.

Fetal size and risk for shoulder dystocia
Fetal presentation
Assessment of fetal heart rate
Indications and alternatives to induction
Synthetic oxytocin, first synthesized in 1955 and identical to the polypeptide hormone produced in the hypothalamus, is one of the most frequently used medications in the United States.
Oxytocin is a proven method of labor induction. ACOG endorses either a ‘low-dose’ or ‘high-dose’ intravenous oxytocin regimen for women undergoing induction of labor.

Low-dose regimens are associated with decreased tachysystole and associated FHR changes. These regimens have a starting dose of 0.5 to 2.0 mU intravenous (IV) infusion per hour increasing by 1 to 2 mU at an interval of 15 to 40 minutes.

High-dose regimens associated with shorter labor, decreased incidence of chorioamnionitis and cesarean section, but increased tachysystole and associated FHR changes. These regimens have a starting dose of 6 mU intravenous (IV) infusion per hour increasing by 3 to 6 mU at an interval of 15 to 40 minutes. The incremental increase is reduced to 3 mU/min in presence of tachysystole and reduced to 1 mU/min with recurrent tachysystole.

The dose is increased until strong contractions occur at 2- to 3-minute intervals, labor progress is normal, or uterine strength reaches 200 montevideo units as recorded by an intrauterine pressure catheter (IUPC).

A meta-analysis of 15 studies of variable quality assessed the utility of discontinuing oxytocin in the active phase of labor. The primary outcome was rate of cesarean delivery, which was lower in the discontinuation group (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.66-0.97). The active phase was longer in the discontinuation group by about 30 minutes, and discontinuation was associated with a reduced rate of tachysystole and non-reassuring fetal heart tracings. There were no differences in neonatal outcomes.
Response to oxytocin depends on cervical favorability, parity, preexisting uterine activity, other medical conditions, and individual biological differences and responses to medication

In one RCT of 193 nulliparous women at term undergoing oxytocin induction, glucose supplementation with 5% dextrose in normal saline vs. normal saline alone significantly reduced total length of labor (499 minutes vs. 423 minutes) without increasing the rate of cesarean or instrumental delivery or newborn APGAR score.
Prostaglandins (PGE2 or PGE1), both vaginal and oral, are effective for both cervical ripening and labor induction.
Vaginal misoprostol (Prostaglandin E1) has been shown to be as effective or superior to dinoprostone gel (prostaglandin E2).

Cervidil, a vaginal insert containing time-released dinoprostone, can be left in place for 12 hours, or until active labor begins. The insert can easily be removed if uterine tachysystole develops, which is an advantage over dinoprostone gel or misoprostol administration.

In one RCT of 245 women with a modified Bishop's score of <7 and a singleton gestation undergoing induction, use of amniotomy the morning after an initial evening dose of PGE2 vaginal gel was associated with a shorter induction of labor-to-birth time compared with the use of a repeat dose of PGE2 (mean difference 5.2 h; 95% CI −2.5 to −7.8).
Misoprostol is as effective as IV oxytocin for inducing labor in women at or near term with either prematurely ruptured membranes or a favorable cervix.

A 25 mcg vaginal dose of misoprostol should be considered the initial dose for cervical ripening and labor induction, with re-administration at 3 to 6 hour intervals. Higher doses (50 mcg) are associated with tachysystole and FHR decelerations.

Oral misoprostol can also be used for labor induction. Cochrane authors found it more effective than placebo at achieving vaginal birth and comparable to vaginal misoprostol and vaginal dinoprostone. Oral misoprostol also results in fewer caesarean sections than oxytocin given for labor inductionThe optimal oral dose of misoprostol has not been determined. One option is 50 mcg orally no more frequently than every 4 hours.
Sublingual/buccal misoprostol has been shown to be as effective as vaginal misoprostol for induction, with similar rates of uterine tachysystole or need for cesarean delivery.
In one RCT of induction among 491 women with a Bishop score of 6 or less, concurrent use of misoprostol-cervical Foley resulted in twice the chance of delivering before either method alone.
As noted above in the “Cervical Readiness” section, prostaglandins are contraindicated in patients with prior cesarean birth, or prior uterine surgeries, due to increased risk for uterine rupture.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 38 cohort and cross-sectional studies found PGE1, PGE2, and mechanical cervical ripening methods to be effective for achieving vaginal delivery in women with previous cesarean delivery and appeared safe among women with only 1 prior cesarean delivery. PGE1 increased risk of uterine rupture among women with ≥2 cesareans compared to women with no prior cesarean section (risk ratio 17.55; 95% CI 3.00-102.8). The absolute risk, however, appeared small at 2.5% vs. 0.08% of women with no prior cesarean section.
Breast stimulation causes uterine contractions. It has not been found to be useful in women with an unfavorable cervix.

Breast stimulation appears beneficial in terms of a reduction in the number of women not in labor after 72 hours, and a reduction in postpartum hemorrhage. Until safety issues are more fully evaluated it should not be considered for use in a high-risk population.
Membrane sweeping is associated with a reduced frequency of a pregnancy continuing beyond 41 weeks and reduces the need for a formal induction.

The examiner’s finger is introduced into the cervical os. Then, the inferior pole of the membranes is detached from the lower uterine segment by a circular movement of the examining finger. This intervention is thought to initiate labor by increasing the local production of prostaglandins.
If desired, membrane sweeping may be initiated in the 39th week of pregnancy.

Artificial rupture of the amniotic membranes is more effective if the cervix is ripe and when combined with intravenous oxytocin. Although widely performed, data on the effectiveness and safety of amniotomy and intravenous oxytocin are lacking.
Data on the effectiveness and safety of amniotomy alone for induction of labor are lacking. No recommendations for clinical practice can be made.
Complications include increased risk of chorioamnionitis (barrier to infection removed), and cord prolapse.
Acupuncture may be of benefit in improving cervical maturity but did not appear to effect other outcomes such as C-section rates and few trials reported safety outcomes.
No universal definition of what constitutes a failed induction.
A low Bishop score is a prognostic factor for failed induction.

An expert workshop defined failed induction as a failure to generate regular contractions approximately every 3 minutes and cervical change after at least 24 hours of oxytocin administration. Membranes should be ruptured, if safe and feasible. After AROM, failure can be considered if regular contraction and cervical change do not occur after at least 12 hours of oxytocin administration.
Cervical ripening interval is not included when determining length of induction or diagnosing induction failure.
